name: Icelandic Plokkfiskur
description: Plokkfiskur, meaning 'plucked' or 'mashed fish', is genuinely a simple dish - real versions have no carrots, celery, tomato, or wine, despite these appearing in many recipes online (a real Icelander's correction confirms this directly). Real technique boils the fish and potatoes completely separately first, then breaks them together with a simple butter-flour-milk béchamel, traditionally also spread on buttered rye bread.
steps_detailed: Boil the potatoes in salted water until tender, 15-18 minutes, then drain and roughly mash.
Separately, gently poach the fish in salted water 8-10 minutes until just cooked through, then drain and flake.
Cook the onion in the butter, 4-5 minutes.
Whisk in the flour, cook 1 minute, then gradually whisk in the milk until thickened into a simple béchamel.
Fold in the mashed potato and flaked fish, breaking everything together into a genuinely mashed, cohesive dish - real plokkfiskur has no other vegetables added.

name: Icelandic Kjötsúpa (Lamb Soup)
description: Kjötsúpa, Iceland's real lamb soup, genuinely skips cream entirely, unlike plokkfiskur - its richness comes from slow-simmered marrow bones, real technique letting the broth simmer long enough to draw out that real depth before the vegetables go in.
steps_detailed: Simmer the lamb with the onion in 3 cups water 40-45 minutes, until the broth has real depth.
Add the carrot and potato, and simmer 15-18 minutes.
Add the cabbage in the last 8-10 minutes, until everything is tender.

name: Icelandic Rúgbrauð (Rye Bread)
description: Rúgbrauð, dense, slightly sweet dark rye bread, traditionally steamed rather than baked (sometimes even buried near a geothermal hot spring), is Iceland's most essential daily bread.
steps_detailed: Mix the rye flour, all-purpose flour, honey, and baking powder with enough water to form a firm, sticky dough.
Pour into a small loaf pan and steam over simmering water 1.5-2 hours until firm - real rúgbrauð is traditionally steamed, not baked.

description: Grilled lamb, seasoned simply with salt and herbs, reflects Iceland's real free-range sheep-farming tradition, real technique keeping the seasoning minimal so the meat's own flavor carries the dish.

Grill or pan-sear, 4-5 minutes per side, until well charred and cooked through.
